ABSTRACT: Electrochemical transformations of epoxides have
emerged as a useful platform for alcohol synthesis , and their
reactivity and selectivity are strongly dictated by the substitutions
of the epoxides. Incorporation of an alkynyl substituent into the
epoxide framework offers a promising yet unexplored avenue toward
highly functionalized different alcohol derivatives posing formidable
challenges in selectivity control. Here , we report an earth-abundant
metal of nickel-catalyzed cross-electrophile coupling between readily
available alkynyl epoxides and aryl /alkenyl halides , enabling the
highly selective synthesis of allenols under mild electrochemical conditions. This protocol exhibits a broad substrate scope , preferential
C−O bond activation over C−X bonds, and a decent chemoselectivity for C −I activation over the C−Br bond, while tolerating a wide
array of synthetically valuable functional groups , such as free hydroxyl, ketone, carboxylate, methoxy, TBS ether, N-Boc, highly strained
cyclopropyl, C═C bonds, C−TMS, C−F bonds, C−Cl bonds, C−Br bonds, and even C −B bonds. Moreover, this methodology may
also apply to the synthesis of allenols bearing pharmaceutical and biologically active moieties , and the downstream derivatizations of
allenol products have also been realized, offering a modular platform for the synthesis of diversified functional structures.
KEYWORDS: alkynyl epoxides, electrosynthesis, nickel catalysis, allenol, cross-electrophile coupling
■ INTRODUCTION
Alcohols are ubiquitous in pharmaceuticals , agrochemicals, fra‐
grances, and flavorings and also serve as indispensable syn‐
thetic intermediates in both laboratory and industrial settings.1,2
Accordingly, the development of efficient and selective synthetic
strategies for functionalized alcohols remains a subject of endur‐
ing interest and practical importance. 3 In organic chemistry ,
epoxides occupy a privileged position owing to their easy prep‐
aration and intrinsic ring strain , which renders them suscepti‐
ble to reductive or nucleophilic ring-opening reactions. 4 On
the other hand , organic electrosynthesis has re-emerged as a
powerful and sustainable platform for redox transformations ,
leveraging electrons as traceless reagents to generate reactive
intermediates under mild and environmentally benign condi‐
tions.5 Electrochemical transformations of epoxides have also
started to attract attention: Lu and co-workers disclosed the
electroreduction of epoxides with carefully tuned proton sources
suppressing hydrogen evolution to enable regioselective access
to Markovnikov alcohols from alkyl epoxides (Scheme 1 A-i)
and anti-Markovnikov alcohols from aryl or benzyl epoxides
(Scheme 1A-ii).6 Qiu et al. and Zhang et al. independently ach‐
ieved electrocarboxylation of aryl epoxide with carbon dioxide ,
affording β-hydroxy carboxylic acids with a very high selectivity
(Scheme 1A-iii).7 These studies collectively underscore the deci‐
sive influence of the substitution on the reactivity and selectivity
of epoxides.8
We envisioned that the incorporation of an alkynyl moiety
could unlock new reactivity patterns of epoxides. The first
thing that came to our mind is their two-component coupling
reactions with organic halides , which may potentially furnish a
new methodology for the syntheses of different functionalized
two-component alcohols, i.e., allenols P1, homopropargylic alco‐
hols P2, or propargylic alcohols P3 (Scheme 1 B, top). This
design is accompanied by formidable challenges (Scheme 1 B,
bottom): (i) the simultaneous presence of two strained C −O
bonds raises the challenge of competing cleavage of two distinct
C−O bonds ; (ii) the incorporation of an alkyne substituent
complicates the regioselectivity, owing to the presence of multiple
reactive sites that can engage in coupling with aryl halides ;9 (iii)
direct electroreduction of the alkynyl epoxide represents a facile
but undesired pathway forming mono-component allenols BP1,
homopropargylic alcohols BP2, and propargylic alcohols BP3 as
reported in the literature;6 (iv) possible allenols P1 or propargyl
alcohols P3 are susceptible to over-reduction 10 or cyclization 11
under electrochemical conditions.

We reasoned that merging transition metal catalysis with
electrochemistry could overcome these obstacles by affording
greater control over bond activation, regioselectivity, and product
distribution.12,13 Such a merger offers complementary advantages:
electrochemistry provides a tunable and sustainable means to
generate reactive intermediates , while transition metal catalysis
governs their selective capture and subsequent transformation.
The synergy between these two activation modes can orchestrate
complex redox sequences that are difficult to achieve by either
approach alone. In this context, Shi et al. demonstrated an elegant
nickel-catalyzed electroreductive coupling of alkyl epoxides with
aryl halides in the presence of isopropyl chloroformate as a CO
surrogate (Scheme 1A-iv).14 Herein, we report the first example
of nickel-catalyzed electrochemical two-component coupling of
alkynyl epoxides with organic halides (Scheme 1C). The current
protocol enables efficient and exclusive synthesis of structurally
diverse allenols,15 a very important class of compounds accommo‐
dating an array of synthetically reactive groups without protection
and deprotection.
■ RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
We first investigated the reaction of alkynyl epoxide 1a and
4-methoxyphenyl iodide 2a in DMF under a constant current of
9 mA in DMF (T able 1). When Pd (dba)2 was employed as the
catalyst in combination with BINAP , no cross-coupled product
was formed with NaBr as the electrolyte together with 2.0 equiv
of Et3N and 3.0 equiv of H 2O (T able 1, entry 1 ). It is interest‐
ing to observe that with DPEphos , DPPB, or BIPHEP as the
ligand (T able 1, entries 2 −4), the reaction of 1a alone afforded
2-phenyl-2,3-heptadienol 4a and enyne product 6a, indicating
the cleavage of the propargylic C −O bond in 1a. When FeCl 3,
FeCl2, or CoCl 2 was used with bipy as the ligand , similar reac‐
tivity was observed (T able 1, entries 5 −7). Interestingly, when
NiCl2·DME was applied, the expected cross coupling product of
tetra-substituted allenol 3aa was obtained in 71% yield with 11%
of enyne 6a (T able 1, entry 8).
A decreased yield was observed when other nickel catalysts ,
such as NiBr2 and NiBr2·DME, were used instead of NiCl2·DME
(T able 2, entries 2 and 3 ). In the absence of nickel catalyst , no
coupling product was obtained (T able 2, entry 4), confirming the
essential role of nickel in this transformation. Bipy proved to be
the most effective ligand, as compared with dtbbpy and 1,10-phen
(T able 2, entries 5 and 6 ). Among the solvents examined , DMF
gave the highest efficiency, outperforming DMA and DMSO
(T able 2, entries 7 and 8 ). Other electrolytes including NaI and
TBABF4 resulted in a poor reactivity (T able 2, entries 9 and 10).
In comparison, when the zinc plate anode was replaced with an
aluminum plate, 3aa was obtained in 49% yield (T able 2, entry 11),
while no product was obtained when carbon felt was used (T able 2,
entry 12). T o our delight, upon fine-tuning the reaction parameters
by increasing the electrode surface area and reaction time while
reducing the equivalents of aryl iodide and triethylamine, the yield

No product formation was observed when the reaction was con‐

afforded the allenol 3aa in a similar yield of 71 % yield (T able 2,

With the optimized conditions in hand , we first evaluated
the substrate scope of aryl halides , and the structures of the
resulting allenol products were unambiguously confirmed through
the X-ray single-crystal analysis of allenol 3ka (Scheme 2). Both
electron-donating and electron-withdrawing groups at the ortho-
(3ac and 3af), meta- (3ab, 3ae, 3bg, and 3ah), and para-positions
(3aa, 3ad, 3aj, 3ak, 3cl, 3cm, 3an, 3ao, 3bp, 3bq, 3ar, 3as, and
3bt) of iodobenzenes are compatible, yielding the corresponding
α-allenols in moderate to good yields exclusively. Steric effects
play a role since the ortho-substituted aryl iodides provided lower
yields (3ac vs 3aa, 3ab; 3af vs 3ad, 3ae). A wide array of functional
groups, such as alkoxyl (3ac and 3ca), phenyl (3ak), chloride
(3ar), trifluoromethyl (3as), nitrile (3bt), naphthyl (3bu), and
pendant benzoheterocycles (3av and 3aw), were well-tolerated
under the current conditions. Notably , substrates with reactive
functional groups such as hydroxyl (3an), Boc-protected amine
(3ao), carboxylate (3bp), and bromide (3ad) all delivered the
α-allenols in 59−67% yields, underscoring the excellent scope of
this strategy.
T o further probe chemoselectivity, bifunctional substrate 2q
bearing both an electrophilic C −I bond and a nucleophilic
C−B bond was evaluated , affording allenol 3bq in 50 % yield.
This outcome highlights the strong preference of those electro‐
chemical conditions for cross-electrophile coupling over electro‐
phile−nucleophile pathways. Gratifyingly , the substrate scope
was further extended to heteroaryl halides. 7-Iodoquinoline (2x)
as well as 3-iodopyridines (2y and 2z) participated smoothly ,
delivering allenols 3ax−3az in good yields. In addition to aryl
iodides, aryl bromides also performed well , affording α-allenols
3aA−3aD smoothly when the electrolyte was switched from NaBr
to NaI. T o facilitate product purification, the reactions of 2A and
2B were carried out on a 0.2 mmol scale under a constant current of
2 mA. Notably, 3-bromoquinoline was also successfully engaged to
furnish product 3aD. Attempts to further extend the scope of aryl
halide substrates to aryl chlorides proved unsuccessful, as neither
p-methoxy nor p-methoxycarbonyl-substituted phenyl chloride
afforded the allenol product (T able S5). However, particularly
noteworthy is the selective reactivity observed with bromophenyl
iodides, where the transformation occurred exclusively at the C−I
bond to furnish the corresponding allenols (3ad−3af) while leav‐
ing the C−Br bond untouched. Such chemoselective activation of
aryl iodides over the C−Br bond in the same molecule represents
a valuable feature for further stepwise elaboration , enabling the
streamlined synthesis of aryl bromide-flanked allenol scaffolds that
can serve as versatile intermediates for further cross-coupling or
functionalization transformations.
The generality  of the reaction was further extended to vinyl
bromides, enabling the synthesis of alkenyl allenes: Cyclic
vinyl bromides, including cyclopentenyl  (3aE) and cyclohex‐
enyl derivatives (3aF), as well as benzene-fused analogues
(3aG and 3aH), underwent smooth conversion under the stand‐
ard conditions.
Next, differently substituted alkynyl epoxides 1 were examined.
The propargylic substituent R2 could be aryl (3da and 3ea), alkyl
(3fa and 3ga), and piperidinyl (3ha), affording products in mod‐
erate yields. The alkynyl epoxide bearing a 4-bromophenyl moiety
(3da) underwent exclusive ring opening at the epoxide site, leaving
the aryl bromide functionality untouched. The C−C triple bond
substituent (R1) can accommodate primary alkyl chains of varying
lengths (3ia, 3ja, 3da, and 3ea) and primary alkyl groups bearing
functional groups such as chloro (3ga), phenyl (3ka), and TBS
ether (3la). Moreover, secondary alkyl groups including the highly
strained cyclopropyl (3ma) and piperidinyl (3na), as well as the
trimethylsilyl group (3oa), are also well-tolerated. Our attempts to
utilize alkynyl epoxides bearing a phenyl on the terminal position

Notably, this transformation was not limited to 1,1-disubstituted
alkynyl epoxides. 1 ,1,2-T risubstituted epoxides also underwent
this transformation efficiently, allowing the formation of secon‐
dary allenols 3pa, 3qa, 3ra, and 3sa in 32 −76% yields. The
stereochemical assignment of allenol 3pa was established through
NOE measurement on its dihydrofuran derivative obtained by
treating (1R*,3Ra*)-3pa with AgNO3 (Scheme 3D; see details in
the Supporting Information, pages S65−S66).16,17 Those of 3qa
and 3ra were assigned analogously (Scheme 3E,F; see details in the
Supporting Information, pages S66−S71).
The reaction exhibits several substrate limitations (Figure S5).
Aryl bromides bearing nitro, acyl chloride, or cyclic amide
groups and acyclic alkenyl iodides were not compatible  under
the standard reaction conditions.  Regarding alkynyl epoxides,
substrates with a bulky tert-butyl group at the propargylic posi‐
tion and terminal alkyne substrate were also unsuitable  for
this transformation.
Moreover, this cross-coupling reaction could also be applied
to the synthesis of complicated allenols containing bioactive or
complex fragments derived from drug molecules and natural prod‐
ucts. As shown in Scheme 3A, various delicate aryl iodides such
as the derivatives of oxaprozin (3aJ), isoxepac (3aK), gemfibrozil
(3aL), indomethacin (3aM), probenecid (3bN), herbicide 2,4-D
(3bO), geraniol (3bP), and phenothiazine (3bQ) were proven
to be effective coupling partners , yielding the corresponding
α-allenols with decent yields and a high regioselectivity . During
our investigation  of the substrate scope, most cross-coupled
allenol products were accompanied  by the formation of enyne
byproducts, which were generated exclusively from the alkynyl
epoxide substrates.
To further  demonstrate  the practicality  of this nickel-
electrocatalyzed protocol, the electrochemical cross-coupling of
5 mmol of alkynyl epoxide 1a and 4-methoxyphenyl iodide 2a was
conducted under constant current electrolysis (45 mA) to provide
the desired allenol product 3aa (0.97 g , 63%) (Scheme 3 B).
Given the synthetic significance  of allenols, the downstream
transformations  have been successfully  realized for the synthesis
of various important structures  (Scheme 3C): In the presence
of a catalytic amount of AgNO 3, 2,3-allenol 3aa underwent
cycloisomerization to produce the dihydrofuran derivative 10;18
iodine-mediated 5- endo-trig cyclization of 3aa resulted in the
formation of 3-iododihydrofuran product 11 with a quantita‐

T o elucidate the mechanistic details of this electrochemical
Ni-catalyzed cross-electrophile coupling, a series of control experi‐
ments were conducted. When a catalytic amount of Ni(cod)2 was
employed under electrolysis conditions , the allenol product 3aa
was obtained in 53% yield, and no electroreduction product allene
4a was detected (Scheme 4A-a). The reaction could also proceed
under non-electrolytic conditions : treatment with 1.0 equiv of
Ni(cod)2 afforded 3aa in 39% NMR yield together with an 11 %
NMR yield of 4a and a 14 % NMR yield of 6a, whereas 3aa
was afforded in 64% yield exclusively upon increasing the nickel
loading to 2.0 equiv (Scheme 4 A-b, entries 2 and 3 ). These
observations suggest that Ni0 species may serve as the catalytically
active species. In addition, the reaction of alkynyl epoxide 1a with
stoichiometric Ni (cod)2 in the absence of aryl iodide afforded
protonated allene 4a in 13% NMR yield, further confirming that
Ni0 species could react with the alkynyl epoxide to form a reactive
organonickel intermediate (Scheme 4A-c).

role as an on-cycle intermediate (Scheme 4B-a). When 2s−Ni

Furthermore, in a competition experiment between 2a and 2s,

T o probe whether allenyl radicals generated via the reductive
activation of alkynyl epoxides 1 are involved in this electrochemical
transformation, we conducted additional electrochemical analyses
using a three-electrode setup to measure the operating cathodic
potentials under different conditions. Under the standard catalytic
conditions, the operating cathodic potential was measured to
be ∼ −1.5 V vs Ag /AgNO3 (Figure S11 ). In contrast , in the
absence of aryl iodide, nickel catalyst, and bipyridine ligand, under
the conditions corresponding to the direct cathodic reduction
of the alkynyl epoxide , the cathodic potential was maintained at
∼ −2.4 V vs Ag /AgNO3 (Figure S10 ). Cyclic voltammogram
(CV) experiments revealed that the reduction potential of alkynyl
epoxide 1a is −2.5 V vs Ag/AgNO3, which displayed an obvious
positive shift to −2.0 V vs Ag /AgNO3 with the assistance of
ZnCl2 (Figure S9). Collectively, these results establish that direct
cathodic reduction of the alkynyl epoxide substrate is not possible
under our catalytic reaction conditions.
Based on these observations, we propose the mechanistic sce‐
nario outlined in Scheme 4C. The catalytically active Ni 0 species
I is generated via electrochemical reduction of the NiII precursor.
This active Ni0 complex I undergoes oxidative addition with the
alkynyl epoxide 1 to afford the allenyl nickel(II) intermediate
II, which is further reduced at the cathode to form the allenyl
NiI species III. Its subsequent oxidative addition with the aryl
halide 2 produces the allenyl aryl NiIII intermediate IV, which
is followed by reductive elimination to yield the cross-coupled
product allenol 3 and the NiI species V. Cathodic reduction of NiI
species V regenerates Ni0, completing the catalytic cycle.
Finally, DFT calculations were carried out to rationalize the
observed regioselectivity (Scheme 4D).23 The calculated energy
barrier for the oxidative addition leading to allene formation is
3.5 kcal /mol lower than that for the alkyne-forming pathway ,
indicating a kinetic preference for the allenyl route. Structural
analysis of transition states TSOA and TSOA’ revealed that the steric
effect governs the pathway selectivity. TSOA’ exhibits significant
steric congestion, with a short H ···H distance (2.07 Å) between
hydroxymethyl and phenyl groups on C1. In contrast, TSOA shows
a much less steric repulsion with a longer H···H distance (2.26 Å),
accounting for the favored formation of the allenyl product.
■ CONCLUSIONS
In conclusion, we have developed an electro-driven
nickel-catalyzed cross-electrophile coupling reaction of alkynyl
epoxides with aryl/alkenyl halides, which allows for the efficient
construction of diverse α-allenols while tolerating a wide range
of synthetically useful functional groups. This method represents

ted functional group tolerance due to the high reactive nature
of the organometallic reagents. Although organoboron reagents
are relatively stable and less reactive, their tedious preparation
using highly reactive reagents further restricts functional group
compatibility. This protocol exhibits high regioselectivity and a
distinctive selectivity profile, featuring preferential C−O bond
activation over C−X bonds as well as pronounced chemoselectiv‐
ity for C−I activation. Notably, this strategy can be applied to the
synthesis of allenols incorporating biologically relevant motifs
under mild conditions and demonstrated that allenols can serve
as valuable intermediates for further synthetic transformations.

15 × 5 mm3) were installed under an argon atmosphere. The resulting
mixture was stirred for 30 min without electricity and subsequently
electrolyzed under a constant current of 9 mA at room temperature.
After the reaction was complete as monitored by TLC after 12 h, the
reaction mixture was transferred with ethyl acetate and quenched with
a saturated aqueous solution of NH4Cl (10 mL). The solid in the
resulting mixture was dissolved with a minimal amount of water. The
organic layer was separated, and the aqueous layer was extracted with
ethyl acetate (20 mL × 3). The combined organic layer was washed
sequentially with H2O and brine, dried over anhydrous Na2SO4, filtered,
and concentrated under reduced pressure. The residue was purified by
column chromatography to afford 3aa (0.2272 g, 74%) (silica gel was
pretreated with 5% (v/v) Et3N in petroleum ether) [eluent: petroleum

epoxide framework ofers a promising yet unexplored avenue toward
highly functionalized diferent alcohol derivatives posing formidable
challenges in selectivity control. Here, we report an earth-abundant
metal of nickel-catalyzed cross-electrophile coupling between readily
available alkynyl epoxides and aryl/alkenyl halides, enabling the

■ INTRODUCTION

Alcohols are ubiquitous in pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals, fra‐
grances, and flavorings and also serve as indispensable syn‐
thetic intermediates in both laboratory and industrial setings.<sup>1,2</sup>
Accordingly, the development of eficient and selective synthetic
strategies for functionalized alcohols remains a subject of endur‐
ing interest and practical importance.<sup>3</sup> In organic chemistry,
epoxides occupy a privileged position owing to their easy prep‐
aration and intrinsic ring strain, which renders them suscepti‐
ble to reductive or nucleophilic ring-opening reactions.<sup>4</sup> On
the other hand, organic electrosynthesis has re-emerged as a
powerful and sustainable platform for redox transformations,
leveraging electrons as traceless reagents to generate reactive
intermediates under mild and environmentally benign condi‐
tions.<sup>5</sup> Electrochemical transformations of epoxides have also
started to atract atention: Lu and co-workers disclosed the
electroreduction of epoxides with carefully tuned proton sources
suppressing hydrogen evolution to enable regioselective access
to Markovnikov alcohols from alkyl epoxides (Scheme 1A-i)
and anti-Markovnikov alcohols from aryl or benzyl epoxides
(Scheme 1A-ii).<sup>6</sup> Qiu et al. and Zhang et al. independently ach‐
ieved electrocarboxylation of aryl epoxide with carbon dioxide,
afording β-hydroxy carboxylic acids with a very high selectivity
(Scheme 1A-iii).<sup>7</sup> These studies collectively underscore the deci
sive influence of the substitution on the reactivity and selectivity
of epoxides.<sup>8</sup>

We envisioned that the incorporation of an alkynyl moiety
could unlock new reactivity paterns of epoxides. The first
thing that came to our mind is their two-component coupling
reactions with organic halides, which may potentially furnish a
new methodology for the syntheses of diferent functionalized
two-component alcohols, i.e., allenols P1, homopropargylic alco‐
hols P2, or propargylic alcohols P3 (Scheme 1B, top). This
design is accompanied by formidable challenges (Scheme 1B,
botom): (i) the simultaneous presence of two strained C−O
bonds raises the challenge of competing cleavage of two distinct
C−O bonds; (ii) the incorporation of an alkyne substituent
complicates the regioselectivity, owing to the presence of multiple
reactive sites that can engage in coupling with aryl halides;<sup>9</sup> (iii)
direct electroreduction of the alkynyl epoxide represents a facile
but undesired pathway forming mono-component allenols BP1,
homopropargylic alcohols BP2, and propargylic alcohols BP3 as
reported in the literature;<sup>6</sup> (iv) possible allenols P1 or propargyl
alcohols P3 are susceptible to over-reduction<sup>10</sup> or cyclization<sup>11</sup>
under electrochemical conditions.

We reasoned that merging transition metal catalysis with
electrochemistry could overcome these obstacles by afording
greater control over bond activation, regioselectivity, and product
distribution.<sup>12,13</sup> Such a merger ofers complementary advantages:
electrochemistry provides a tunable and sustainable means to
generate reactive intermediates, while transition metal catalysis
governs their selective capture and subsequent transformation.
The synergy between these two activation modes can orchestrate
complex redox sequences that are dificult to achieve by either
approach alone. In this context, Shi et al. demonstrated an elegant
nickel-catalyzed electroreductive coupling of alkyl epoxides with
aryl halides in the presence of isopropyl chloroformate as a CO
surrogate (Scheme 1A-iv).<sup>14</sup> Herein, we report the first example
of nickel-catalyzed electrochemical two-component coupling of
alkynyl epoxides with organic halides (Scheme 1C). The current

resulting allenol products were unambiguously confirmed through

electron-donating and electron-withdrawing groups at the ortho-
(3ac and 3af), meta- (3ab, 3ae, 3bg, and 3ah), and para-positions

functional groups such as hydroxyl (3an), Boc-protected amine
(3ao), carboxylate (3bp), and bromide (3ad) all delivered the
α-allenols in 59−67% yields, underscoring the excellent scope of
this strategy.

To further probe chemoselectivity, bifunctional substrate 2q
bearing both an electrophilic C−I bond and a nucleophilic
C−B bond was evaluated, afording allenol 3bq in 50% yield.
This outcome highlights the strong preference of those electro‐
chemical conditions for cross-electrophile coupling over electro‐
phile−nucleophile pathways. Gratifyingly, the substrate scope
was further extended to heteroaryl halides. 7-Iodoquinoline (2x)
as well as 3-iodopyridines (2y and 2z) participated smoothly,

delivering allenols 3ax−3az in good yields. In addition to aryl
iodides, aryl bromides also performed well, afording α-allenols
3aA−3aD smoothly when the electrolyte was switched from NaBr
to NaI. To facilitate product purification, the reactions of 2A and
2B were carried out on a 0.2 mmol scale under a constant current of
2 mA. Notably, 3-bromoquinoline was also successfully engaged to
furnish product 3aD. Atempts to further extend the scope of aryl
halide substrates to aryl chlorides proved unsuccessful, as neither
p-methoxy nor p-methoxycarbonyl-substituted phenyl chloride
aforded the allenol product (Table S5). However, particularly
noteworthy is the selective reactivity observed with bromophenyl
iodides, where the transformation occurred exclusively at the C−I
bond to furnish the corresponding allenols (3ad−3af) while leav‐
ing the C−Br bond untouched. Such chemoselective activation of
aryl iodides over the C−Br bond in the same molecule represents
a valuable feature for further stepwise elaboration, enabling the
streamlined synthesis of aryl bromide-flanked allenol scafolds that
can serve as versatile intermediates for further cross-coupling or
functionalization transformations.

■ CONCLUSIONS

In conclusion, we have developed an electro-driven
nickel-catalyzed cross-electrophile coupling reaction of alkynyl
epoxides with aryl/alkenyl halides, which allows for the efficient
construction of diverse α-allenols while tolerating a wide range
of synthetically useful functional groups. This method represents

a compelling alternative to conventional approaches that rely
on preformed nucleophiles such as Grignard reagents,<sup>24−26</sup> orga‐
nozinc species,<sup>27,28</sup> organoboron reagents,<sup>29−32</sup>
and terminal
alkynes.<sup>33,34</sup> These traditional allenol synthesis sufers from limi‐
ted functional group tolerance due to the high reactive nature
of the organometallic reagents. Although organoboron reagents
are relatively stable and less reactive, their tedious preparation
using highly reactive reagents further restricts functional group
compatibility. This protocol exhibits high regioselectivity and a
distinctive selectivity profile, featuring preferential C−O bond
activation over C−X bonds as well as pronounced chemoselectiv
ity for C−I activation. Notably, this strategy can be applied to the
synthesis of allenols incorporating biologically relevant motifs
under mild conditions and demonstrated that allenols can serve
as valuable intermediates for further synthetic transformations.
